facts.statement: The Rodrigues rail became extinct in the mid-18th century.
facts.quote: extinct: mid-18th century

facts.statement: The species name of the Rodrigues rail is leguati.
facts.quote: species: leguati

facts.statement: The Rodrigues rail was first described by Alphonse Milne-Edwards in 1874.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Milne-Edwards, 1874

facts.statement: The Rodrigues rail was an extinct rail species endemic to the island of Rodrigues in the Mascarenes.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues rail (Erythromachus leguati), also known as Leguat's gelinote or Leguat's rail, is an extinct species of the rail family that was endemic to the Mascarene island of Rodrigues.

facts.statement: Subfossil remains were discovered and linked to historical accounts in 1874.
facts.quote: Subfossil remains were later discovered and correlated with the old accounts in 1874

facts.statement: The bird possessed a long beak that curved downwards.
facts.quote: The beak was long and curved downwards.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues rail was flightless and fed on tortoise eggs.
facts.quote: It was flightless and fed on tortoise eggs.

facts.statement: The bird was attracted to red objects, a trait humans exploited to hunt it.
facts.quote: It was described as being attracted to red objects, which humans exploited while hunting it.

facts.statement: The species is believed to have gone extinct in the mid-18th century due to predation by introduced cats and hunting.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues rail is believed to have become extinct in the mid-18th century mainly because of predation by introduced cats and hunting.

facts.statement: Hugh Edwin Strickland drew attention to the bird in François Leguat's 1708 memoir in 1848.
facts.quote: In 1848, the English zoologist Hugh Edwin Strickland called attention to a bird mentioned in the French traveller François Leguat's 1708 memoir

facts.statement: Alphonse Milne-Edwards described subfossil bones in 1874 after receiving them from Alfred Newton.
facts.quote: In 1874, the French zoologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards described subfossil bird bones from Rodrigues he had received via the British ornithologist Alfred Newton

facts.statement: Milne-Edwards linked Leguat's account to a sternum, tarsometatarsus, and skull fragment found in the Plaine Corail caves.
facts.quote: Milne-Edwards connected Leguat's account with three bones (a sternum, a tarsometatarsus, and a fragmentary skull) found in caves of the Plaine Corail region, Rodrigues.

facts.statement: Albert Günther and E. Newton described additional fossils, including skulls, in 1879.
facts.quote: In 1879, more fossils, including skulls, were described by the zoologists Albert Günther and E. Newton

facts.statement: Geoffroy Atkinson questioned the bird's existence in 1921 by doubting the truth of Leguat's memoir.
facts.quote: In 1921, the American linguist Geoffroy Atkinson questioned the bird's existence, in an article that doubted the veracity of Leguat's memoir.

facts.statement: James Greenway suggested in 1967 that the bird was actually a purple swamphen, an idea not accepted by other experts.
facts.quote: The American ornithologist James Greenway suggested in 1967 that Leguat's description referred to wind-blown purple swamphens, since the word grey is sometimes used synonymously with blue in old descriptions. This idea has not been accepted by other commentators.

facts.statement: The species is generally placed in the genus Erythromachus but has sometimes been grouped with the red rail in Aphanapteryx.
facts.quote: It is generally kept in its own genus, Erythromachus, but has sometimes been assigned to the genus Aphanapteryx along with its close relative the red rail (A. bonasia) of Mauritius; their relationship with other rails is unclear.

facts.statement: Günther and E. Newton confirmed in 1879 that the bird belonged to the rail family.
facts.quote: In 1879, more fossils, including skulls, were described by the zoologists Albert Günther and E. Newton, who confirmed that the bird was a rail

facts.statement: Günther and E. Newton synonymized the two rails into one genus in 1879 due to skeletal similarities.
facts.quote: Günther and E. Newton first generically synonymised the two in 1879 because of their skeletal similarities.

facts.statement: Jean Piveteau found skull differences in 1945 that justified separating the two species into different genera.
facts.quote: In 1945, the French palaeontologist Jean Piveteau found skull features of the two species different enough for generic separation

facts.statement: Storrs L. Olson suggested in 1977 that the two species should be kept separate due to considerable divergence.
facts.quote: In 1977, the American ornithologist Storrs L. Olson stated that though the two species were similar and derived from the same stock, they had also diverged considerably, and should possibly be kept separate.

facts.statement: Bradley C. Livezey could not determine the evolutionary affinities of the two rails in 1998.
facts.quote: The American ornithologist Bradley C. Livezey was unable to determine the affinities of the Rodrigues and red rail in 1998

facts.statement: Julian Hume suggested the ancestors arrived in the Mascarenes no earlier than the middle Miocene, though it may have been more recent.
facts.quote: He suggested their ancestors could have arrived on the Mascarenes during the middle Miocene at the earliest, but it may have happened more recently.

facts.statement: Specialized rails like the Rodrigues rail could evolve flightlessness and distinct features in less than 1 to 3 million years.
facts.quote: Flightlessness can evolve rapidly in rails, sometimes repeatedly within the same groups, as in Dryolimnas, so the distinctness of the Rodrigues and red rails may not have taken long to evolve; some other specialised rails evolved in less than 1–3 million years.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues rail measured approximately 35 cm in length and had proportionally longer wings than the red rail.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues rail was about 35 cm long, smaller than the red rail, but with proportionally longer wings.

facts.statement: The bird likely weighed at least 500 grams.
facts.quote: It may have weighed at least 500 g.

facts.statement: Its plumage was bright grey, possibly with white flecks.
facts.quote: It had bright grey plumage, perhaps flecked with white.

facts.statement: Its cranium was slightly elongated, convex in all directions, and compressed from top to bottom when viewed from the side.
facts.quote: The cranium of the Rodrigues rail was slightly elongated, convex in every direction, and compressed from top to bottom in side-view.

facts.statement: The skull was medium-sized for Mascarene rails, measuring 38 mm in length and 20 mm in width.
facts.quote: The cranium was medium-sized among Mascarene rails, 38 mm long and 20 mm wide.

facts.statement: The nostril opening was exceptionally long, accounting for 66% of the beak's total length.
facts.quote: The narial (nostril) opening was very long, 66% of the rostrum's length.

facts.statement: The thigh bone was very robust with a curved shaft, measuring between 56 and 63 mm long.
facts.quote: The femur (thigh-bone) was very robust, with a curved shaft, and ranged from 56 to 63 mm in length.

facts.statement: Contemporary accounts state the bird fed on the eggs of three extinct giant tortoise species that lived on Rodrigues.
facts.quote: According to Tafforet's account, the Rodrigues rail fed on the eggs of the now extinct Cylindraspis tortoises, three species of which lived on Rodrigues.

facts.statement: A phalanx bone of the Rodrigues rail was discovered among fossilized tortoise egg remains.
facts.quote: The phalanx bone of a Rodrigues rail has been found among the egg remains.

facts.statement: It likely fed on worms like Kontikia whartoni and Geonemertes rodericana by probing leaf litter or rotting wood.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues rail probably fed on worms, such as Kontikia whartoni and the now extinct Geonemertes rodericana, by probing leaf-litter or rotting wood.

facts.statement: The bird was reportedly attracted to the color red, though the reason for this behavior remains unknown.
facts.quote: Like the red rail, it was said to be attracted to the colour red, but the significance of this is unknown.

facts.statement: All six endemic Mascarene rail species, including this one, went extinct due to human activities.
facts.quote: All six endemic species of Mascarene rails are extinct, caused by human activities.

facts.statement: The species was first documented by Leguat in a memoir published in 1708.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues rail was first recorded by Leguat in his 1708 memoir

facts.statement: The genus was established by Milne-Edwards in 1874.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Milne-Edwards, 1874

facts.statement: The species was described by Milne-Edwards in 1874.
facts.quote: species_authority: Milne-Edwards, 1874

facts.statement: Researchers noted significant variation in beak shape and length among specimens but debated whether this indicated sexual dimorphism or individual size differences.
facts.quote: Günther and Newton stated that the examined beaks varied greatly in size and shape; some specimens had short and almost straight beaks, while others had much longer beaks (up to one third longer) that were prominently curved. These writers were unsure whether this was related to the overall size of an individual bird or to sexual dimorphism.

facts.statement: In 2003, Livezy could not confirm that beak differences reflected sexual dimorphism but considered it probable.
facts.quote: Livezy was unable to confirm the idea that the differences in the beaks reflected dimorphism in 2003, but thought it probable.

facts.statement: A 2019 examination by Hume found no differences in beak curvature among available specimens.
facts.quote: Hume examined all available upper beaks in 2019, but found no differences in curvature.

facts.statement: Hume and Walters suggested the species went extinct within a decade of cat introduction around 1750, though the exact cause remains debated.
facts.quote: Hume and the British ornithologist Michael Walters stated in 2012 that this must have taken a toll on the rails through hunting and deforestation, but their rapid disappearance was probably caused by cats introduced to control the rats around 1750, and the species may have gone extinct within a decade.

facts.statement: Cheke argued in 2013 that the species survived rats, went extinct primarily due to cats, and was assisted by hunting, noting there was no deforestation at the time.
facts.quote: Cheke responded in 2013 that there was no deforestation at the time, the species appears to have survived the rats, and that cats were the main culprits, assisted by hunting.

facts.statement: Erythromachus leguati, known as the Rodrigues rail, is an extinct bird belonging to the Rallidae family and was endemic to Rodrigues island in the Mascarene Islands.
facts.quote: El rascón de Rodrigues (Erythromachus leguati) es un ave extinta, de la familia Rallidae que era endémica de las islas Mascareñas en la isla de Rodrigues, ubicada al este de Madagascar en el océano Índico.

facts.statement: The bird had grey plumage, a red bill, red legs, and reddish coloration around its eyes.
facts.quote: Es descrito con un plumaje de color gris, el pico rojo, de piernas rojas, y una coloración de tonos rojizos alrededor del ojo.

facts.statement: Bills varied between specimens, with some being straight and others twisted, though the reason for this variation is unknown.
facts.quote: El pico iba variando entre los distintos especímenes, encontrándose algunos rectos y otros torcidos, pero la razón del porque variaban los picos es desconocida.

facts.statement: Reports suggest the bird was attracted to red objects, which made it easier for humans to catch them.
facts.quote: Según relatos, sentía una atracción hacia los objetos rojos, por el cual a los humanos se les hizo más fácil atraparlos.

facts.statement: The bird was first described by François Leguat, a French Huguenot refugee stranded on Rodrigues in 1691, and was named leguati in his honor.
facts.quote: El pájaro fue primero descrito por François Leguat, un francés Huguenotes refugiado en marooned en Rodrigues en 1691, y fue nombrado leguati en su honor.

facts.statement: A second description was made by Julien Tafforet, another refugee stranded on the island in 1726.
facts.quote: La segunda descripción es realizada por Julien Tafforet, también en el refugio marooned en la isla en 1726.

facts.statement: The bird was also described using subfossil material in 1874.
facts.quote: Además fue descrito por material subfosil en 1874.

facts.statement: It was a plump, flightless rail with light grey plumage, possibly spotted with white, a red bill and legs, and a red naked area around its eyes.
facts.quote: El rascón de Rodrigues era un rascón regordete, no volador, de plumaje gris claro, quizá manchado de blanco, con un pico y patas rojas, y un área roja y desnuda alrededor de sus ojos.

facts.statement: It was slightly smaller than its closest relative, the Rodrigues rail, and was about the size of a chicken, though its exact length is unknown.
facts.quote: Era algo más pequeño que su pariente más cercano, el rascón rojo. La longitud exacta del ave es desconocida, pero era del tamaño de un pollo.

facts.statement: Its skull measured 38 millimeters long by 20 millimeters wide, and its bill was 77 millimeters long.
facts.quote: Su cráneo medía 38 milímetros (1,5 pulg.) de largo por 20 milímetros (0,79 pulg.) de ancho, y el pico era de 77 milímetros (3,0 pulgadas) de largo.

facts.statement: It fed on invertebrates and possibly small vertebrates, and during the nesting season of the extinct giant tortoises, it dug up and fattened their eggs.
facts.quote: El rascón de Rodrigues se alimentó de invertebrados, posiblemente pequeñosvertebrados, y en la época de anidación de las extintas tortugas Cylindraspis, desenterraron y engordaron sushuevos.

facts.statement: Its vocalizations included a continuous whistle and an alarm call resembling a hiccup.
facts.quote: Sus vocalizaciones eran un silbido continuo, y tenía una llamada de alarma, como un hipo.

facts.statement: They had no fear of humans because they evolved in the absence of predators, allowing hunters to catch them in large numbers.
facts.quote: No tenían miedo de los humanos porque habían evolucionado en ausencia de depredadores, permitiendo a los cazadores cogerlos en gran número.

facts.statement: It is sometimes assigned to the genus Aphanapteryx along with its close relative the Rodrigues rail, but they are generally considered species of different genera.
facts.quote: Es a veces asignada al género Aphanapteryx, junto con su pariente cercano el rascón rojo (A. bonasia). De la isla Mauricio, pero son generalmente considerados especies de distinto género.

facts.statement: The generic name Erythromachus was coined by Milne-Edwards from Greek words for 'red' and 'battle', referring to its behavior toward red objects, and the specific name honors Leguat.
facts.quote: Milne-Edwards acuñó el nombre genérico Erthyromachus de las palabras griegas para "rojo" y "batalla", en referencia a su comportamiento hacia los objetos rojos, y el nombre concreto es en honor a Leguat.

facts.statement: The synonym Miserythrus, meaning 'red' and 'aversion', was coined by Alfred Newton in 1893, also referring to this behavior.
facts.quote: la sinonimia Miserythrus, de "rojo" y "aversión", estuvo acuñada por el inglés ornithologo Alfred Newton en 1893, también refiriéndose a este comportamiento.

facts.statement: Zoologists Edward Newton and Albert Günther first synonymized them generically in 1879 due to skeletal similarities.
facts.quote: Los zoólogos Edward Newton y Albert Günther primero los sinonimizaron genéricamente en 1879 debido a sus semejanzas esqueléticas.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that due to geographic locations and nasal bone morphology, they may have been related to the genera Gallirallus, Dryolimnas, Atlantisia, and Rallus.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido que debido a las ubicaciones geográficas de estas especies y la morfología de los huesos nasales, pueden haber estado relacionados con los géneros Gallirallus, Dryolimnas, Atlantisia y Rallus.

facts.statement: It had slightly larger wings than the Rodrigues rail, but the proportions of its legs, pelvis, and sacrum were also similar.
facts.quote: El rascón de Rodrigues tenía alas algo mayores que el rascón rojo, pero las proporciones de las piernas de la especie, la pelvis y el sacro también eran similares.

facts.statement: It also had a proportionally longer humerus, a wider and shorter skull, and longer, lower nostril openings than the Rodrigues rail, differing considerably in plumage based on early descriptions.
facts.quote: También tenía un húmero proporcionalmente más largo, un cráneo más ancho y más corto, y tenían los orificios de la nariz más largos y más bajos que el rascón rojo, del cual difería considerablemente en plumaje, basado en descripciones tempranas.

facts.statement: American ornithologist James Greenway suggested that Leguat's description referred to the common crab, but this has not been accepted by other authors.
facts.quote: El americano ornithologo James Greenway sugirió que la descripción de Leguat se refirió acalamón común. Esto no ha sido aceptado por otros autores.

facts.statement: It is unknown whether the variation in bill size and shape was related to sexual dimorphism or individual variation.
facts.quote: Se desconoce si esto estaba relacionado con eldimorfismo sexual o con la variación individual.

facts.statement: Its pelvis was large and strongly built in proportion to the bird's size.
facts.quote: La pelvis era grande y fuertemente construida en proporción al tamaño del pájaro.

facts.statement: The French astronomer Alexandre Guy Pingré reported in his 1763 report that the bird was extinct in 1761.
facts.quote: El astrónomo francés Alexandre Guy Pingré escribió en su informe de 1763 que el ave estaba extinta en 1761.

facts.statement: The fat of birds that had fed on turtle eggs was bright orange and used as a remedy for people recovering from illness.
facts.quote: La grasa de las aves que se habían alimentado de huevos de tortuga era naranja brillante y se utilizó como un remedio para las personas que se recuperan de la enfermedad.

facts.statement: The genus Erythromachus was named by Milne-Edwards in 1874.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Erythromachus (genus), Milne-Edwards 1874

facts.statement: The genus Erythromachus belongs to the family Rallidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Rallidae

facts.statement: The type species for the genus Erythromachus is Lophopsittacus bensoni.
facts.quote: Type species: Lophopsittacus bensoni

facts.statement: The genus Erythromachus lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Holocene to Holocene (0.0117 to 0 million years ago)
